title: Static or dynamic dispatch?

rows.label: Who picks the function
values: The compiler, from the types it sees
The running program, from the object the call is made on

rows.label: What a call costs
values: A direct call, or none at all once inlined
A load from a table (vtable, itable) and an indirect call

rows.label: Optimization
values: The optimizer can inline and optimize across the call
Blocks inlining, unless a JIT sees one type in practice and inlines speculatively

rows.label: Compiled code
values: One copy per type (monomorphization), so bigger binaries and slower builds

rows.label: Mixed-type collections
values: Yes: a `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` holds circles and squares together

rows.label: Types added later
values: Must exist when the program is compiled
Plugins, subclasses and test fakes work without recompiling the caller

rows.label: In code
values: Overloads, C++ templates, Rust generics (`fn f<T: Trait>`), Go generics (partly)
C++ `virtual`, Rust `dyn Trait`, Go interfaces, Java and C# interfaces and virtual methods, Python and JavaScript method calls

tip: Default to static dispatch for code on the hot path where every type is known, and to dynamic dispatch where flexibility matters more than a few nanoseconds per call: plugin systems, heterogeneous lists, dependency injection, tests. Many designs mix them: a generic inner loop called from a `dyn` interface at the edge, or a C++ template that shares its non-generic core through a base class. Measure before switching; JITs such as HotSpot often remove the cost of virtual calls that only ever see one type.
